tts: Rolex makes more than a million watches a year. And yet, walk into a store and ask for a popular steel model, and you'll probably be told to join a waitlist. The company has no shareholders, isn't listed on any stock exchange, and doesn't publish its results. It's owned by a charitable foundation. And the most Swiss of all watch brands was started by a German orphan, in London. So how did a made-up word become the most recognized luxury brand on the planet? Along the way, we'll meet a swimmer in the English Channel, a watch at the bottom of the ocean, and a foundation that answers to no one. Let's wind it back to the beginning.

Hans Wilsdorf was born in Bavaria in eighteen eighty-one. By the age of twelve he had lost both parents, and he was sent to boarding school, where he learned languages and business. His first real job was at a company in Switzerland that exported watches, and there he fell in love with precision. He never trained as a watchmaker. He was a salesman with an obsession. In nineteen-oh-three, he moved to London. Two years later, at just twenty-four, he started a company with his brother-in-law, Alfred Davis. Wilsdorf and Davis didn't make movements. They bought small, accurate Swiss movements, put them in cases, and sold them in Britain. And they bet on something most people laughed at: the wristwatch.

Back then, real men carried pocket watches. Wristwatches were seen as jewelry for women, and they were fragile and inaccurate. Wilsdorf wanted to prove the opposite, and he sold accuracy, not decoration, which was unusual at the time. In nineteen-oh-eight, he needed a name, something short that would fit on a dial and sound the same in every language. He later claimed it came to him on the top deck of a London bus: Rolex. In nineteen ten, one of his watches became the first wristwatch to earn an official Swiss chronometer certificate. And in nineteen fourteen, the Kew Observatory in Britain gave a Rolex a class A precision certificate, a rating usually reserved for marine chronometers on ships.

Then the First World War changed everything. Soldiers in the trenches discovered that a watch on the wrist was far more practical than one in a pocket. But Britain raised import duties on luxury goods, and a German-born businessman in London faced growing suspicion. So in nineteen nineteen, Wilsdorf moved the company to Geneva, and it became Montres Rolex, which simply means Rolex Watches in French. The movements kept coming from the same partner in the town of Bienne. Rolex finally bought that movement maker outright in two thousand four, almost a century later.

Dust and water were the enemies of every watch. In nineteen twenty-six, Rolex solved both with the Oyster: a case sealed like an oyster shell, with a screw-down crown and back. The little crown you twist to wind the watch seals against a gasket, like a submarine hatch. To prove it, Wilsdorf gave one to Mercedes Gleitze, a young English typist and swimmer. In nineteen twenty-seven, she spent about ten hours in the freezing English Channel, and the watch kept running. Wilsdorf paid for the entire front page of the Daily Mail to tell the world. According to the company, jewelers then displayed Oysters in fish tanks in their shop windows. Four years later, Rolex added the Perpetual rotor, a weight that winds the watch as your wrist moves.

Then came the tool watches. In nineteen forty-five, the Datejust showed the date in a little window. In nineteen fifty-three, the expedition that first reached the top of Everest carried Oyster Perpetuals. The same year brought the Submariner, a dive watch, and the Explorer. In nineteen fifty-five, the GMT-Master was made for Pan Am pilots crossing time zones. In nineteen sixty, a Rolex strapped to the outside of the submersible Trieste went down almost eleven kilometers to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, and came back working. In twenty twelve, director James Cameron repeated the dive, with another Rolex on board. Many of these models are still made today, and from across the room they look almost the same as they did seventy years ago. That's on purpose: Rolex changes its designs very, very slowly.

Now, the strangest part of the story. In nineteen forty-four, Wilsdorf's wife died. He had no children. A year later, he created the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, and when he died in nineteen sixty, it took control of Rolex. That means there's no founder family cashing out, no shareholders demanding quarterly growth, and no public accounts. The foundation is known to fund charitable projects, many of them in Geneva, but even those details are rarely discussed. A foundation like this has no owners at all. It can't be sold like a family business, and it has to follow the purpose its founder wrote down. This structure lets Rolex think in decades, not quarters, and it makes the company almost impossible to buy.

That patience shows in how Rolex makes watches. It does almost everything itself, at several sites in Switzerland. It even runs its own foundry, casting its own gold alloys. It makes its own steel alloy, which it calls Oystersteel, and it tests finished watches again after casing, to a tighter standard than the official chronometer test. It sells new watches only through authorized dealers, and it never floods the market. During the watch boom of twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two, some steel models traded online for far more than their store price, and waitlists grew to years. Then prices on the secondhand market cooled. Rolex responded by moving into retail itself: in twenty twenty-three, it agreed to buy Bucherer, its largest retail partner, and it launched its own certified pre-owned program.

So how big is Rolex? Since it publishes nothing, analysts have to estimate it from trade data and dealer surveys. The latest estimates put Rolex sales at around eleven billion Swiss francs a year, by some estimates roughly a third of the entire Swiss watch industry. No other watch brand comes close. And because the company has no shareholders to pay, much of that money can go back into the business, into new machines, new buildings, and into keeping production deliberately tight. Prices go up almost every year, and demand still runs ahead of supply.

So, look at the whole journey. An orphan from Bavaria. A made-up word on a London bus. A watch that survived ten hours in the English Channel, the top of Everest, and the deepest point of the ocean. And a company that belongs to no one, and is in no hurry at all. And if a dealer ever calls to say your watch has finally arrived, now you know the story behind the little crown on the dial. Maybe that's the real secret of Rolex. In a world that wants everything now, it sells the one thing it can never make faster: time.
